(CNN) -- A federal judge has stayed what would be the nation's first military execution since 1961, saying the U.S. soldier -- who was convicted of rape and murder two decades ago -- should have more time to pursue a federal appeal. Pvt. Ronald Gray has been on the military's death row at Fort Leavenworth, Kansas, since 1988. A court-martial panel sitting at Fort Bragg, North Carolina, unanimously convicted him of committing two murders and other crimes in the Fayetteville, North Carolina, area and sentenced him to death. Last month, the Army said Gray was scheduled to be executed by lethal injection December 10 at the Federal Correctional Complex in Terre Haute, Indiana. But in an order issued November 26, U.S. District Judge Richard Rogers of Kansas said that a stay is necessary so Gray can pursue his federal appeal. Rogers ruled on a motion filed by Gray's attorneys, who asked for time to challenge the legality of his convictions and sentence. Government attorneys have asked Rogers to reconsider his decision, saying that Gray seeks a stay "apparently based on the premise that at some point he will identify a new legal issue or discover new evidence" upon which to appeal and that Gray "continues to delay unnecessarily." Gray has had ample time to appeal, the Justice Department attorneys said. In a response filed Tuesday, Gray's defense attorneys point out that the U.S. Supreme Court declined to hear his appeal in March 2001, and "since then, it has taken the Department of the Army, the Department of Defense, the Department of Justice and the Office of the President over seven years to approve as final Private Gray's sentence of death. The significant constitutional issues presented on the face of Private Gray's case ... have obviously troubled the decision-makers, as evidenced by the years they had his case under advisement." President Bush approved Gray's death sentence in July, making it final, defense attorneys write in the filing. Inmates sentenced to death in state and federal courts are given a year to file federal appeals after their death sentence becomes final, they claim, and members of the military under death sentences should receive the same consideration. "Private Gray is seeking federal habeas court review for the first time and he has not delayed commencing this action," defense attorney Thomas Bath wrote. "In fact, until the president approved his death sentence, there was no action available." Gray was convicted of raping and killing a female Army private and a civilian near his post at Fort Bragg. He also was convicted of the rape and attempted murder of another fellow soldier in her barracks at the post. Military and civilian courts both found Gray responsible for the crimes, which were committed between April 1986 and January 1987. Gray pleaded guilty to two murders and five rapes in a civilian court and was sentenced to three consecutive and five concurrent life terms. The general court-martial at Fort Bragg then tried him and in April 1988 convicted him of two murders, an attempted murder and three rapes. Bush's July action, the Army said in a statement at the time, followed "completion of a full appellate process, which upheld the conviction and sentence to death." Members of the U.S. military have been executed throughout history, but just 10 have been executed with presidential approval since 1951 under the Uniform Code of Military justice, the military's modern-day legal system. The Army has also sought Bush's authorization to execute another condemned soldier, Pvt. Dwight Loving, who was convicted of killing and robbing two cab drivers in 1988. The last U.S. military execution was in 1961, when Army Pvt. John Bennett was hanged for raping and attempting to kill an 11-year-old Austrian girl. Bennett was sentenced in 1955. The U.S. military hasn't actively pursued an execution for a military prisoner since President Kennedy commuted a death sentence in 1962. Nine men are currently on military death row. CNN's Mike Mount contributed to this report.

**WASHINGTON (CNN) —** A federal judge has granted a stay of execution for a U.S. Army soldier on military death row at Fort Leavenworth, halting what would have been the U.S. military’s first execution in more than 60 years. 

U.S. District Court Judge Arthur Gaines issued the emergency order late Tuesday, pausing the execution of Sgt. 1st Class Marcus Vance just weeks before he was scheduled to face lethal injection. The stay allows Vance’s legal team to pursue a federal *habeas corpus* petition, arguing that his original court-martial suffered from severe constitutional errors, including ineffective assistance of counsel and suppressed evidence.

Vance was convicted by a military panel in 2014 for his role in the premeditated murder of two fellow soldiers and an Afghan civilian during a deployment in Kandahar Province. 

"The gravity and permanence of the death penalty demand that every avenue of federal judicial review be thoroughly exhausted," Judge Gaines wrote in his ruling. "Allowing an execution to proceed while substantial constitutional questions remain unresolved would constitute an irreparable injury."

### A Rare and Complex Legal Process

Military death penalty cases are among the most complex and heavily litigated in the American legal system. Unlike civilian capital cases, a military execution cannot move forward without direct approval from the President of the United States, who serves as the commander-in-chief. 

While former President Donald Trump authorized Vance’s execution order during his final days in office—a mandate later upheld by the Department of Defense under the Biden administration—Tuesday's ruling shifts the battlefield from the military justice system to the civilian federal courts.

Vance is currently one of only four inmates housed on death row at the United States Disciplinary Barracks (USDB) at Fort Leavenworth, Kansas, the military’s only maximum-security facility for service members. Among those also housed there is Nidal Hasan, the former Army psychiatrist who killed 13 people in the 2009 Fort Hood shooting.

"Military justice moves meticulously, and for good reason," said Rachel Vance-Lowe, a senior legal analyst and former Army Judge Advocate General (JAG) officer. "The threshold for carrying out a capital sentence in the armed forces is exceptionally high, which is why we have seen decades pass without a single sentence being carried out."

### The Last Military Execution: 1961

The U.S. military has not executed a service member in over six decades. 

The last military execution took place on **April 13, 1961**, when Army Private John A. Bennett was hanged at Fort Leavenworth. 

Bennett was convicted by a court-martial for the 1954 rape and attempted murder of an 11-year-old Austrian girl while stationed in Austria. President John F. Kennedy approved the execution after reviewing the case, making Bennett the final inmate to be executed under military authority. 

In 1986, the U.S. military officially replaced hanging with lethal injection as its sole method of execution, aligning its protocols with those of federal civilian capital punishment. However, no service member has been executed since the change was adopted.

### What Lies Ahead

Tuesday's stay means Vance will remain at Fort Leavenworth indefinitely as his legal team prepares oral arguments for the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Tenth Circuit. 

"We are deeply grateful that the court recognized the necessity of full judicial review," said lead defense counsel Michael Connelly in a statement to CNN. "Sgt. Vance’s trial was compromised from the start, and we intend to prove in federal court that his death sentence is unjust."

Representatives for the U.S. Army Legal Services Agency declined to comment directly on the active litigation, but stated that the Department of Defense "remains committed to upholding the rule of law and ensuring due process in all military justice proceedings."

Legal experts say the federal appeal process could take years to resolve, virtually guaranteeing that military death row will remain untouched for the foreseeable future.

**TOPEKA, Kansas (CNN)** — A federal judge has issued a stay of execution for Army Pvt. Ronald A. Gray, temporarily halting what would have been the U.S. military’s first execution in nearly five decades, court documents revealed Wednesday.

U.S. District Judge Richard Rogers granted the emergency stay to allow time for the court to consider Gray’s petition for a federal habeas corpus review—a legal process that Gray’s defense attorneys argue was improperly delayed and denied during his military appeals.

Gray, a former Army cook, was set to die by lethal injection on December 10 at the Federal Correctional Complex in Terre Haute, Indiana. The military does not maintain an active execution facility and relies on the federal death row chamber in Terre Haute for capital punishment cases.

President George W. Bush approved the execution order in July, marking the first time a president had authorized a military execution since Dwight D. Eisenhower signed off on the execution of Army Pvt. John A. Bennett in 1961. 

Gray was convicted by a military court-martial in 1988 for a brutal crime spree committed while he was stationed at Fort Bragg, North Carolina. He was found guilty of two murders, an attempted murder, and three rapes involving both military personnel and civilians in the area surrounding the base. He later pleaded guilty in a civilian court to two additional murders and another rape.

In his ruling, Judge Rogers highlighted the complex constitutional questions surrounding the delays in Gray’s habeas corpus review. Defense attorneys contend that Gray’s trial counsel failed to adequately present evidence of his severe mental illness and that civil federal courts have a constitutional duty to review military death penalty cases before an execution can proceed. 

"The court believes that petitioner should be given the opportunity to present his claims," Rogers wrote in the order, noting that executing Gray before a full habeas review could lead to an irreversible violation of his constitutional rights.

Military prosecutors had argued against the stay, asserting that Gray’s case had already been exhaustively reviewed through the military court system over the past two decades. 

The Army stated it will comply with the federal court's order while justice department attorneys review the judge's ruling. Gray will remain on military death row at the United States Disciplinary Barracks at Fort Leavenworth, Kansas, while the stay remains in effect.

*CNN's Mike Mount and Mary Snow contributed to this report.*

**Justice in Limbo: The Story of Ronald Gray and the Rarity of the U.S. Military Death Penalty**

In July 2008, President George W. Bush signed an execution warrant for U.S. Army Private Ronald A. Gray. It was a momentous and historic act: no American president had approved the execution of a U.S. service member in over half a century. 

Gray, convicted of a horrifying spree of rapes and murders committed in the late 1980s near Fort Bragg, North Carolina, appeared to be days away from lethal injection. Yet, more than fifteen years after that presidential sign-off—and nearly four decades after his arrest—Ronald Gray remains alive on military death row at the United States Disciplinary Barracks in Fort Leavenworth, Kansas.

The prolonged saga of Ronald Gray highlights the extraordinary legal complexities of capital punishment under military law, the fierce defense strategies that have repeatedly stayed his execution, and the profound rarity of military executions in modern American history.

---

### The Crimes and the Court-Martial

Between 1986 and 1987, Ronald Gray, a specialist stationed at Fort Bragg, waged a campaign of violence against women in the Fayetteville, North Carolina area. His victims included both civilian women and female military personnel. 

In 1988, Gray was tried by a military court-martial. He was convicted of two murders, an attempted murder, and three rapes. Separately, in a civilian North Carolina state court, he pleaded guilty to two additional murders and five rapes, receiving consecutive life sentences. 

For the crimes tried under the Uniform Code of Military Justice (UCMJ), the military panel sentenced Gray to death. Under military law, a capital sentence triggers a rigorous, multi-tiered process of automatic reviews that takes decades to navigate—a reality that would soon turn Gray’s sentence into one of the longest legal odysseys in American jurisprudence.

---

### Why Defense Lawyers Fought for a Stay

Since 1988, defense attorneys representing Gray have waged a persistent legal battle to keep him off the gurney. Their efforts have centered on procedural rights, claims of ineffective assistance of counsel, and complex questions regarding Gray’s mental health.

#### 1. Exhaustion of Habeas Corpus Rights
When President Bush signed the execution warrant in July 2008, setting an execution date for December of that year, Gray’s defense team immediately filed for a stay of execution in federal civilian court. 

They argued that Gray had not yet been afforded the opportunity to seek *habeas corpus* review in a civilian federal court—a constitutional right granted to death row inmates. Up to that point, Gray’s appeals had occurred entirely within the military legal system (including the Army Court of Criminal Appeals and the Court of Appeals for the Armed Forces). A U.S. District Judge agreed, granting a stay of execution to allow Gray to challenge his conviction in civilian courts.

#### 2. Ineffective Assistance of Counsel
A central pillar of the defense’s argument has been that Gray’s trial attorneys failed him during the original 1988 court-martial. Defense lawyers argued that his original counsel failed to adequately investigate and present mitigating evidence regarding Gray's severe childhood abuse, neurological deficits, and psychological trauma. 

Under Supreme Court precedent, a defendant facing the death penalty is entitled to a defense team that thoroughly investigates mitigating circumstances that might persuade a jury to spare their life. Gray’s post-conviction attorneys argued that if the original military panel had known the extent of his psychiatric and neurological damage, they might have opted for a sentence of life without parole instead of death.

#### 3. Mental Incompetency and Brain Damage
Over the years, defense attorneys presented medical evaluations suggesting that Gray suffers from organic brain damage, major depressive disorder, and severe personality disorders. Under U.S. constitutional law (specifically the landmark Supreme Court ruling in *Ford v. Wainwright*), it is illegal to execute an inmate who is mentally incompetent and lacks a rational understanding of why they are being executed.

Defense lawyers repeatedly sought stays to conduct thorough psychiatric evaluations, arguing that forcing an incompetent man to face execution violated the Eighth Amendment's protection against cruel and unusual punishment.

#### 4. The 2016 Resumption and Re-Stay
In 2016, after years of federal lower-court proceedings, the U.S. District Court lifted the stay, allowing the Army to move forward with execution preparations once again. However, Gray’s defense team quickly appealed to the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Tenth Circuit, securing yet another emergency stay. The courts ruled that complex questions regarding federal jurisdiction over military capital cases required deeper judicial review, bringing the execution to a halt once again.

---

### The Extreme Rarity of Military Executions

To understand why Ronald Gray’s case has stalled for decades, one must understand just how exceedingly rare capital punishment is within the United States Armed Forces.

The last military execution took place on **April 13, 1961**, when Army Private John A. Bennett was hanged at Fort Leavenworth for the rape and attempted murder of an 11-year-old Austrian girl. Since Bennett’s execution, no American service member has been put to death by the military.

Several unique factors contribute to the dormancy of the military death penalty:

#### 1. The Requirement of Presidential Authorization
Unlike civilian capital cases, where a state governor or state attorney general handles the execution order, article 71(a) of the UCMJ requires the President of the United States to personally approve a military execution. 

This creates a massive political hurdle. Presidents are often hesitant to sign execution warrants due to political risks, international scrutiny, and the legal quagmire that inevitably follows. Prior to George W. Bush signing Gray’s warrant in 2008, no president had authorized a military execution since Dwight D. Eisenhower in 1957.

#### 2. The Dual Jurisdiction Paradox
Because the military operates its own justice system alongside civilian state and federal courts, capital cases often involve jurisdictional ping-pong. An inmate must exhaust appeals within the specialized military justice pipeline before transferring their appeals to civilian federal courts (District Court, Circuit Court of Appeals, and ultimately the U.S. Supreme Court). This dual-track system effectively doubles the time required to litigate appeals.

#### 3. A Tiny Death Row Population
Military death row is exceptionally small. Currently, only four men sit on military death row at Fort Leavenworth (including Nidal Hasan, the perpetrator of the 2009 Fort Hood shooting). Because capital court-martials are rare, military appellate courts proceed with extreme caution, knowing that any mistake could overturn a high-profile case.

---

### Conclusion: A System in Stasis

The case of Ronald Gray highlights a profound paradox in American military law: while the UCMJ retains the death penalty for the most heinous offenses, the system is so burdened by procedural safeguards, mandatory executive approvals, and protracted appeals that executing an inmate has proven nearly impossible in the modern era.

For the families of Gray’s victims, the endless legal stays represent a delayed and agonizing search for finality. For defense lawyers and civil rights advocates, the delays demonstrate the essential safeguards required to ensure constitutional rights are protected, even when defending individuals accused of horrific acts.

As Ronald Gray remains at Fort Leavenworth in his late 50s, his case serves as a living symbol of an American military capital punishment system that exists on paper, but has been functionally frozen for over six decades.
